Something waits on the other side's turn. One of their pieces could attack several targets at once, a fork.
A fork sat inside another move, one piece reaching several targets together. This move leaves it untouched.
The piece on that line cannot leave it. It is pinned to its king, and stepping off would expose the king.
Look along the line to the king. The other side can pin a piece there, and a pinned piece cannot leave without exposing its king.
Another move held a pin to the king. The pinned piece would have been fixed to its line, unable to step off without exposing the king behind it.
Two pieces stand on one line. The attack meets the front one first, and when it steps aside, the piece behind is exposed. A skewer.
The front piece is not alone on its line. The other side can try a skewer, and moving that front piece could expose what stands behind it.
A stronger move had a skewer in it. Had the front piece stepped aside, the one behind it would have been exposed.
The defender is the target. Capture it, and what it protected loses that protection.
One defender is holding something in place. The other side can now capture it, and what it guards could be left without protection.
A different move could have captured a defender. What it guarded would have stood without that protection.
The king is walled in by its own pieces. This move uses that: a back-rank mate pattern.
The king's own pieces stand where it would need to escape. That gives the other side a route to a back-rank mate.
A back-rank mate was available, the king hemmed in by its own pieces. This move goes another way, and the mate goes unplayed.
A pawn has a road to the last rank. When it arrives, it becomes a new piece. That is the aim here.
One of their pawns now has a way toward the last rank. This gives the other side a chance to promote it.
A stronger move opened the way for a pawn to reach the last rank and promote. This move does not take that road.
One piece steps out of the line. Behind it, another piece was already aimed. That is the discovered attack.
One of their pieces is screening another. If it steps aside, the piece behind can attack. This allows that discovered attack.
Another move had a discovered attack: one piece stepping aside to uncover a threat from the piece behind. After this move, that threat stays hidden.
Two threats arrive from one move. That is a double attack, two attacks working together.
Two threats could arrive together now. This gives the other side a double attack, both made with one move.
A stronger move made two attacks at once. That double attack goes unused here.
A defender is drawn away from its post. What it was covering is left open. That is the deflection.
One defender carries an important task. The other side can now draw it away, a deflection, and that task would go uncovered.
Another move could have drawn a defender away from its task. That deflection is not used.
A piece stood with no guard. The idea is simply to take it.
Another move could have taken an undefended piece. Nothing was guarding it, and this move does not take it.
A piece is left behind with no guard. The other side can take it.
Notice what just left. This move takes away a piece's only real defender, and the other side can capture what it left behind.
The threat arrived with the opponent's last move. It is still waiting, unanswered, and a piece can now be captured.
The capture is only the first half. Then the recapture takes a piece of greater value. Count the whole exchange.
A minor piece is off its starting square now. It is in play.
A different move would have developed a minor piece, lifting it from its starting square.
The rook stands on an open file. No pawn of either color is on it.
No pawns stand on the file occupied by White's rook. It is an open file now.
No pawns stand on the file occupied by Black's rook. It is an open file now.
Another move would have placed a rook on an open file, empty of pawns of either color.
The better move would have left White's rook on a file with no pawns at all. An open file, in the position not chosen.
The better move would have left Black's rook on a file with no pawns at all. An open file, in the position not chosen.
The rook now stands on a semi-open file. None of its own pawns are there, and at least one enemy pawn still is.
Along White's rook file, the friendly pawns are absent. Enemy pawns remain. The file is semi-open.
Along Black's rook file, the friendly pawns are absent. Enemy pawns remain. The file is semi-open.
With another move, a rook would have stood on a semi-open file, clear of its own pawns, with an enemy pawn still on it.
The better move would have given White's rook a semi-open file. No friendly pawn there, though enemy pawns would remain.
The better move would have given Black's rook a semi-open file. No friendly pawn there, though enemy pawns would remain.
This pawn has no enemy pawn ahead of it, on its own file or either file beside it. It is passed.
White has a passed pawn now. No enemy pawn lies ahead on its file or the neighboring files. Other obstacles may remain.
Black has a passed pawn now. No enemy pawn lies ahead on its file or the neighboring files. Other obstacles may remain.
Another move would have made a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or either neighboring file.

There was another possibility. The better move would have given Black a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or neighboring files.
The passed pawn moves forward. It was passed before; now it stands nearer the last rank.

An already passed pawn advances. The distance to promotion is shorter now.
Another move would have pushed the passed pawn forward, nearer the last rank.
A pawn stands alone now. No friendly pawn is on either file beside it. It is isolated.

Black's pawn is isolated now. The neighboring files hold no friendly pawns. Piece support is a different matter.

Another move would have given the king a new legal flight square.
The king steps aside to castle, and the rook crosses over to stand beside it.
The king slips to one side, and the rook moves in close. Castled.

Another move would have captured a bishop, breaking the other side's bishop pair.

The king's defenses no longer hold. The other side can force checkmate now. Follow the attack in, one move at a time.
A forced checkmate was there. This move leaves it behind. Going back, the finish can still be found.
Checkmate is left waiting now. The other side's very next move can deliver it.
A shadow settles over the position. The side that played this move can force checkmate now, whatever the defense. There is more to come first.
The forced checkmate lingers. This move keeps it from fading. Other moves must pass before the end.
Another move would have forced checkmate sooner. That one was passed by. The mate is still forced, only slower in coming.
The last door closes. Past the reply, whatever it is, the side that moved has checkmate, and no answer keeps it out.
The mate against the side that moved was already certain. Nothing could have turned it away. This move only calls it in early; the best defense would have kept it waiting.
The mate against the side that moved could not be stopped, and it still comes. Nothing in the search puts it off longer. The sensible defense, nothing more.
The offered material can be taken. In the line that was checked, taking it does not refute the sacrifice.
Every other move that was checked was losing. This one alone kept the position playable.
Behind every other move checked, a losing position was waiting. This one alone avoided it.
The danger was already there for every other move checked. Only this move left the position playable.

This was the lone keeper of the advantage. The other moves that were checked were losing.
